note: Repo-agnostic, language-agnostic rule manifest for the test-driven-development discipline — red-green-refactor, Kent Beck's three laws, test-first as design, arrange-act-assert, one-assertion-per-behavior, the test pyramid, test doubles (dummy/fake/stub/spy/mock), classical vs mockist TDD, test determinism, coverage as a tool, property-based testing, snapshot/golden testing, regression-test discipline, and safe refactoring under green — distilled from Fowler's testing articles/bliki, xunitpatterns.com (Meszaros), Robert C. Martin's Three Laws, Kent Beck's own Test Desiderata essay, and the Hypothesis/Jest practitioner docs. The .md is authoritative and unchanged; this indexes every actionable rule, typed checkable|judgment|principle, with predicate/reviewer_criterion. Any agent implementing a feature or bugfix via TDD, in any language, applies this manifest — distinct from the Genesis-specific test-driven-determinism expertise in .genesis/, which encodes this repo's own toolchain and gates.

rules.text: Never write production code without a failing test that demands it. The mechanism is the red-green-refactor cycle: write a test for the next bit of behavior, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor — repeated in a tight loop, driven from a test list written up front. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html.]

Test-first is a design technique, not verification bolted on afterward. Writing the test before the code forces you to consider the desired behavior and interface before implementation — this tends to produce smaller units, looser coupling, and clearer interfaces, especially when tests are written against public behavior rather than implementation details. [VERIFIED, Wikipedia Test-driven_development 'Potential benefits', citing Beck (2003) — secondary source summarizing Beck's own claim.]

Determinism is non-negotiable — a suite that lies sometimes is worse than no suite. A test that passes sometimes and fails sometimes 'without any noticeable change in the code, tests, or environment' destroys the value of the whole regression suite, because people stop trusting any of it, not just the flaky test. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html.]

The macro loop has exactly three steps, repeated: (1) write a test for the next bit of functionality you want to add; (2) write the functional code until that test passes; (3) refactor both new and old code to make it well structured. Commonly summarized as Red → Green → Refactor. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html.]

predicate.spec: each unit of new behavior is introduced by first writing a failing test for it, then writing the minimum code to pass it, then refactoring — in that order, per behavior.

rules.text: Before the loop starts, write out a list of test cases you expect to need. Pick one, run red-green-refactor on it, then pick the next — adding new items to the list as they occur to you along the way. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html.]

predicate.spec: a running list of anticipated test cases exists and is consumed one at a time via red-green-refactor, with new items added to the list as they're discovered mid-work rather than worked ad hoc.

rules.text: TDD operates at three nested cycle granularities: a macro-cycle (the test list, tackled test-by-test), a milli-cycle — the minute-by-minute Red/Green/Refactor loop, run once per complete unit test — and a nano-cycle, the second-by-second Three Laws (§2), iterated roughly a dozen times inside one milli-cycle. [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html.]

The philosophy behind Red-Green-Refactor: a limited mind cannot pursue correct behavior and correct structure at the same time, so get behavior right first (green), and only then restructure. Robert C. Martin traces this to what he calls 'Kent Beck's original injunction': 'Make it work. Make it right. Make it fast.' [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html — Martin's citation of Beck, not Martin's own coinage.]

predicate.spec: within one red-green-refactor cycle, structural improvement (refactor) is deferred until after the test passes (green); behavior and structure are never pursued as one combined step.

rules.text: The Three Laws of TDD, verbatim, from Robert C. Martin's original statement of the rule: 1. 'You are not allowed to write any production code unless it is to make a failing unit test pass.' 2. 'You are not allowed to write any more of a unit test than is sufficient to fail; and compilation failures are failures.' 3. 'You are not allowed to write any more production code than is sufficient to pass the one failing unit test.' [VERIFIED, butunclebob.com/ArticleS.UncleBob.TheThreeRulesOfTdd — 'The Three Laws of TDD.', quoted exactly.] Martin's later, reworded retelling of the same three rules in The Cycles of TDD ('You must write a failing test before you write any production code...') is a paraphrase, not a second verbatim source — an earlier pass of this guide incorrectly labeled that paraphrase as verbatim. [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html, citing programmer.97things.oreilly.com/wiki/index.php/The_Three_Laws_of_Test-Driven_Development.]

predicate.spec: no production code is written before a failing test exists for it; a test is never extended past the point needed to fail/not-compile before returning to production code; production code is never extended past what the current failing test requires.

rules.text: Attribute precisely: the Three Laws were codified by Robert C. Martin as a distillation of the fine-grained discipline he experienced pair-programming with Kent Beck — they are Martin's formulation of the practice, not a verbatim quotation from Beck's own book. Do not cite them as Beck's own words. [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html — 'the fine grained structure ... I experienced while working with Kent so long ago'.]

The Three Laws force line-by-line granularity: they are iterated roughly a dozen times to produce one complete unit test. Breaking law 2 or law 3 is a violation of TDD discipline even if the end result is the same code, because the sequencing — not just the destination — is the point. [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html.]

predicate.spec: a completed unit test can be traced through multiple small write-test/write-code alternations rather than one large test followed by one large implementation chunk.

rules.text: Because the test is written before the code, the developer must consider the desired behavior and interface first. This tends to produce smaller units of code, looser coupling, and clearer interfaces — especially when the tests exercise public behavior rather than implementation detail. [VERIFIED, Wikipedia Test-driven_development 'Potential benefits', citing Beck (2003) — secondary source.]

predicate.spec: tests assert against a unit's public behavior/interface rather than its private implementation details.

rules.text: Keeping the unit under test small has two claimed, concrete benefits: reduced debugging effort (a failure localizes to a smaller piece of code) and self-documenting tests (small test cases are easier to read and understand). [VERIFIED, Wikipedia Test-driven_development 'Keep the unit small', citing Pathfinder Solutions — secondary source.]

predicate.spec: units under test are kept small (class or small function-group scale) rather than large, multi-responsibility modules.

rules.text: 'Fake it till you make it' — Kent Beck's own strategy from Test-Driven Development by Example for getting from red to green fast: return a literal, hard-coded value first, then generalize under the next test that forces you to. This is a legitimate, deliberate TDD move, not a shortcut to be embarrassed about — it keeps each nano-cycle (§2) small. [VERIFIED, Wikipedia Test-driven_development 'Development style', naming the principle from Beck's book — secondary source for attribution.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: When a fully general implementation isn't obvious, is a hard-coded/faked pass used deliberately to reach green quickly, with generalization deferred to the next test that actually forces it, rather than either stalling on the design or over-generalizing early?

rules.text: TDD's rapid red-green-refactor cycle relies primarily on unit tests that avoid process boundaries, network connections, or external dependencies so they execute quickly; where the code under development genuinely depends on something external, TDD encourages substituting a test double (§7) to keep the unit test fast and isolated. [VERIFIED, Wikipedia Test-driven_development 'Test isolation' — secondary source.]

predicate.spec: unit tests driving the TDD cycle do not cross process boundaries, hit the network, or depend on external systems; such dependencies are replaced with test doubles.

rules.text: The by-product of doing this well is self-testing code: comprehensive automated tests written alongside the functional software such that a single command executes them all, and passing gives real confidence hidden bugs would have been illuminated. You can also reach self-testing code by writing tests after the code — what matters is that the tests exist and pass, not strictly how you got there. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfTestingCode.html.]

predicate.spec: the full test suite is invokable via a single command, and a passing run is treated as grounds for confidence that hidden bugs would have surfaced.

rules.text: Structure every test in four phases, executed in sequence: fixture setup (establish the prior state the SUT needs), exercise SUT (actually invoke the behavior under test), result verification (check the expected outcome), fixture teardown (housekeeping — restore the world). Clearly separating the four phases makes a test's intent far easier to see. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Four%20Phase%20Test.html.]

predicate.spec: each test is organized into a visible setup phase, an exercise phase, a verification phase, and a teardown phase, in that order.

rules.text: A common shorthand for the first three phases is the 'Arrange, Act, Assert' mnemonic: set up the test data, call the method under test, assert the expected results. Fowler attributes the mnemonic to Bill Wake's originating article '3A – Arrange, Act, Assert' (xp123.com). A BDD-flavored alternative is the given/when/then triad. Both keep tests short, consistent, and easy to read regardless of test level. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'Test Structure', which links the mnemonic directly to xp123.com/articles/3a-arrange-act-assert/ as Wake's article; xp123.com itself returned a fetch-tool error in this session, so the attribution is verified via Fowler's citation of it, not a direct read of Wake's page.]

predicate.spec: a test's body reads as arrange-then-act-then-assert (or given-when-then) with the three parts visually distinguishable, at any test level.

rules.text: Do not let setup or teardown logic obscure the exercise/verify lines that actually carry the test's meaning — from a 'tests as documentation' standpoint, the housekeeping phases are deliberately the least important ones for a reader trying to understand what behavior is being verified. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Four%20Phase%20Test.html, citing the 'Tests as Documentation' goal.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Reading the test, is it immediately obvious which lines are exercising the SUT and which are asserting the outcome, with setup/teardown kept visually and logically out of the way rather than interleaved into the core logic?

rules.text: Because assertion calls can raise exceptions, wrap the exercise+verify block in a try/finally (or the language equivalent) so fixture teardown still runs even when an assertion fails — otherwise a failing assertion silently leaks state into the next test. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Four%20Phase%20Test.html — 'Example: Four Phase Test (Inline)'.]

predicate.spec: fixture teardown for a test executes even when the exercise or verification phase raises/throws, e.g. via try/finally or an equivalent guaranteed-cleanup construct.

rules.text: 'Assertion Roulette' is a named test smell: 'it is hard to tell which of several assertions within the same test method caused a test failure.' A test with many assertions and no distinguishing failure message forces a reader to re-run and single-step just to find out what broke. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Assertion%20Roulette.html.]

predicate.spec: a failing test's output identifies which specific assertion/behavior failed without requiring the reader to re-run or step through the test to find out.

rules.text: The Eager Test symptom that causes it: a test exercises several methods of the system under test, or calls the same method several times, interleaved with fixture setup and assertions for each — effectively several tests welded into one. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Assertion%20Roulette.html — 'Cause: Eager Test'.]

predicate.spec: a single test method does not interleave multiple rounds of (setup → exercise → assert) for distinct SUT behaviors; each such round is its own test.

rules.text: Verify one behavior per test. Several assertions that check different facets of a single logical outcome (e.g., three fields of one returned object) are fine — they still fail together, for the same reason. What to avoid is exercising multiple distinct SUT behaviors in one test method. [INFERRED, synthesizing xunitpatterns.com's Assertion Roulette and Eager Test entries.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Do all assertions in a given test check facets of one single logical behavior/outcome, rather than spanning multiple distinct SUT behaviors that happen to be checked in the same test method?

rules.text: The test pyramid (Mike Cohn, Succeeding with Agile) is a way of thinking about how different kinds of automated tests should be combined into a balanced portfolio: many more low-level unit tests than high-level, broad-stack tests driven through a GUI. Cohn's original three layers, bottom to top, are Unit Tests → Service Tests → User Interface Tests. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html and martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html.]

predicate.spec: the test suite's composition, from most to fewest tests, runs low-level/unit → service/integration → high-level UI/broad-stack, not the reverse.

rules.text: Even critics of the exact shape agree on two takeaways from Cohn's pyramid: write tests at different granularities, and write fewer tests as you climb to higher-level, more integrated levels. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'The Test Pyramid'.]

predicate.spec: the test suite contains tests at more than one granularity, and the count of tests strictly decreases (or does not increase) as granularity gets more end-to-end.

rules.text: The ice-cream-cone anti-pattern is the inversion: an approach built mainly around record-and-playback UI automation looks easy at first, but such UI-driven tests are slow, often license-locked to particular machines, hard to run headless, and more prone to non-determinism, which further undermines trust in them even when written with good practice. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html.]

predicate.spec: the test suite's shape is not inverted — it does not consist mainly of slow, UI-driven record/playback tests with few or no low-level unit tests underneath.

rules.text: Distinguish solitary unit tests (every collaborator replaced with a mock/stub, for perfect isolation) from sociable unit tests (collaborators left real unless they're slow or have big side effects) — terms coined by Jay Fields. Neither is universally correct; using both, situationally, is normal practice. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'Sociable and Solitary', citing Jay Fields.]

predicate.spec: unit tests are consciously classifiable as solitary (all collaborators doubled) or sociable (real collaborators used unless slow/side-effecting), and the codebase does not dogmatically force one style everywhere.

rules.text: Testing terminology is genuinely contested — 'integration test' means different things to different teams, as do 'component test,' 'service test,' and 'broad-stack test.' Don't get hung up on winning the label debate; agree on team-consistent terms and be explicit about what each level covers. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'The Confusion About Testing Terminology'.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Does the team use its own consistently-defined test-level vocabulary (documented or well understood), rather than assuming a term like 'integration test' means the same thing to everyone by default?

rules.text: End-to-end tests give the highest confidence that the software works, and are also the most fragile: they are 'notoriously flaky and often fail for unexpected and unforeseeable reasons,' driven by browser quirks, timing issues, animations, and unexpected popup dialogs. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'End-to-End Tests'.]

predicate.spec: end-to-end tests exist and are treated as a small, high-value, expected-to-be-flakier layer rather than the suite's primary confidence mechanism.

rules.text: Fowler's Test Pyramid bliki explicitly points readers, in its own 'Further Reading' section, to the Google Testing Blog's 'Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests' (Mike Wacker, 2015) as further support for the pyramid's shape. That cross-reference itself — title, author, and Fowler's one-line summary — is directly verified on Fowler's page; the Google post's own extended body text was not independently fetched and re-verified in this session. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html — 'Further Reading': 'The Google Testing Blog expands on why you shouldn't rely on end-to-end tests.'] The stronger characterization sometimes attached to this reference — that fewer, cheaper, faster low-level tests catch more, sooner, more reliably than a large end-to-end layer can — is this guide's own synthesis of Fowler's stated rationale elsewhere in his testing corpus (Fast Feedback as a deployment-pipeline value; 'push your tests as far down the test pyramid as you can'), not a verified quotation of the Google Testing Blog post's own argument. [INFERRED, synthesizing martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'Putting Tests Into Your Deployment Pipeline' and 'Avoid Test Duplication' — explicitly not the Google post's own verified body text.]

predicate.spec: a decision to add more coverage defaults toward lower-level tests first, treating 'add another end-to-end test' as the higher-cost, later resort rather than the default.

rules.text: Test Double is the generic umbrella term (Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns) for any pretend object substituted for a real one during testing. The specific vocabulary — dummy, fake, stub, spy, mock — is Meszaros's, adopted because it distinguishes real differences rather than being interchangeable jargon. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html.]

predicate.spec: when a test-time substitute object is discussed, it is named by its specific kind (dummy/fake/stub/spy/mock) rather than using 'mock' as a catch-all for every kind of test double.

rules.text: Dummy Object — passed only because a method signature requires a parameter neither the test nor the SUT actually cares about. A dummy should never actually be used by the receiver, so it needs no real implementation. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Test%20Double.html and xunitpatterns.com/Dummy%20Object.html.]

predicate.spec: a dummy argument/object is passed to satisfy a required parameter and is never actually invoked or read by the code under test.

rules.text: Fake Object — a working, but much simpler/lighter implementation than the real thing it replaces, unsuitable for production but functionally real enough to let the SUT run against it. Unlike a stub or mock, a fake needs no per-test canned-response configuration. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Fake%20Object.html and xunitpatterns.com/Test%20Double.html.]

predicate.spec: a fake provides a genuinely working, simplified implementation of the dependency's behavior, installed once, without per-test response configuration.

rules.text: Test Stub — a control point for the SUT's indirect inputs: it returns pre-programmed answers so the test can drive the SUT through otherwise-hard-to-trigger behaviors. A stub is the right choice when you need to control inputs but have no need to verify indirect outputs. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Test%20Stub.html.]

predicate.spec: a stub supplies canned return values to control the SUT's indirect inputs, and the test does not assert on calls made to the stub itself.

rules.text: Test Spy — an observation point: like a stub, it may still supply canned responses, but it additionally captures the SUT's indirect outputs as they occur, for the test to inspect and verify afterward (state-style verification after the fact). [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Test%20Double.html and xunitpatterns.com/Test%20Spy.html.]

predicate.spec: a spy records the calls/outputs it receives from the SUT, and the test asserts against that recorded data after the exercise phase completes, rather than the double asserting during the call.

rules.text: Mock Object — replaces a dependency with a test-specific object whose expectations are declared before the SUT is exercised, and which itself verifies that it was called correctly. This is the mechanism for behavior verification: the mock, not a later assertion, determines pass/fail for the interaction. [VERIFIED, xunitpatterns.com/Mock%20Object.html and martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html.]

predicate.spec: expectations on a mock double are set up before the SUT is exercised, and the mock itself (not a post-hoc assertion) determines whether it was used correctly.

rules.text: The dividing line across all five kinds is state verification vs. behavior verification: a stub-based test checks the final state of the SUT after exercising it; a mock-based test checks that the right calls happened, verified by the double itself. Mock objects always use behavior verification; a stub-style double extended to do so is what Meszaros calls a Test Spy. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — 'The Difference Between Mocks and Stubs'.]

predicate.spec: every test-double-based test is classifiable as using state verification (checking the SUT's resulting state) or behavior verification (checking that specific calls occurred), and that classification is consistent with which double kind is in play.

rules.text: Pick the double by what the test actually needs to know: a dummy when a parameter is structurally required but semantically irrelevant; a fake when the SUT needs something real-feeling but too heavy/unavailable for the test environment; a stub when you need to control indirect inputs and don't care how the SUT called it; a spy or mock when the interaction itself — not just the resulting state — is the thing under test. [INFERRED, synthesized across xunitpatterns.com's Test Double / Dummy / Fake / Stub / Spy / Mock pages.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: For each test double introduced, does its kind (dummy/fake/stub/spy/mock) match what the test actually needs to observe or control, rather than defaulting to 'mock' regardless of whether behavior verification is actually needed?

rules.text: Classical TDD: use real collaborator objects wherever practical, and reach for a test double only when using the real thing would be awkward (slow, non-deterministic, hard to construct). The specific kind of double matters less to a classicist than simply avoiding the awkward dependency. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — 'Classical and Mockist Testing'.]

predicate.spec: under a classical-TDD test, collaborators are real objects except where a specific one is awkward (slow/non-deterministic/hard to construct), in which case only that one is doubled.

rules.text: Mockist TDD: always substitute a mock for any collaborator with interesting behavior, real or awkward, because the interaction itself is treated as part of the specification. Behavior Driven Development (BDD) is an important offshoot of the mockist style. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — 'Classical and Mockist Testing'.]

predicate.spec: under a mockist-TDD test, every collaborator with interesting behavior is replaced with a mock, regardless of whether the real collaborator would have been convenient to use.

rules.text: Mockist tests are more coupled to implementation: they check the SUT's outbound calls, so changing how a method talks to its collaborators tends to break the test even with identical externally-observed behavior. A classic test only cares about the SUT's final state, so it survives more refactoring untouched. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — 'Coupling Tests to Implementations'.]

predicate.spec: a refactor that preserves a unit's externally observed state/behavior but changes how it calls its collaborators is more likely to break a mockist (behavior-verification) test than a classical (state-verification) test for the same unit.

rules.text: There is no universally correct answer between classical and mockist TDD; Fowler himself, a self-described classic TDDer, presents both fairly. A concrete signal for trying mockist testing: losing time debugging tests that fail without clearly indicating where or why. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — 'So should I be a classicist or a mockist?'.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is the classical-vs-mockist choice for a given codebase/team made deliberately based on observed pain (e.g. unclear test failures favoring mockist, or refactoring brittleness favoring classical), rather than assumed as a fixed house style with no reconsideration?

rules.text: Kent Beck's Test Desiderata names the load-bearing properties directly: Isolated — 'tests should return the same results regardless of the order in which they are run'; Composable — 'if tests are isolated, then I can run 1 or 10 or 100 or 1,000,000 and get the same results'; Deterministic — 'if nothing changes, the test result shouldn't change'; Automated — 'tests should run without human intervention.' [VERIFIED, Kent Beck, 'Test Desiderata,' medium.com/@kentbeck_7670/test-desiderata-94150638a4b3.]

predicate.spec: tests produce the same pass/fail result regardless of execution order or how many other tests ran alongside them, given no code/environment change, and run without any manual/human step.

rules.text: A test is non-deterministic exactly when 'it passes sometimes and fails sometimes, without any noticeable change in the code, tests, or environment' — failures for such a test are seemingly random, and that randomness corrodes trust in the entire suite, not just that one test. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html.]

predicate.spec: no test in the suite exhibits pass/fail results that vary across identical code/test/environment states.

rules.text: The first response to a non-deterministic test is to quarantine it into a separate suite immediately, so it stops eroding confidence in the healthy suite — but fix quarantined tests quickly, bounded by a hard limit (e.g. a fixed count, or a time limit such as one week) so quarantine cannot silently become a graveyard. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Quarantine'.]

predicate.spec: a detected flaky test is moved out of the main/trusted suite promptly, into a quarantine area bounded by an explicit count or time limit that forces its cleanup rather than allowing indefinite residence.

rules.text: Lack of isolation is the most common cause of non-determinism — one test leaving data behind can corrupt a later test that assumes a clean starting state. Prefer rebuilding starting state from scratch over relying on each test to clean up after itself: a rebuild failure localizes cleanly to the offending test, whereas a cleanup failure makes a different test fail. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Lack of Isolation'.]

predicate.spec: each test establishes its own starting state from scratch (rather than depending on state left by a prior test or on that prior test's cleanup step succeeding).

rules.text: Always wrap the system clock behind a seam that tests can substitute — a 'clock stub' set to and frozen at a particular time — so time-dependent behavior becomes controllable and repeatable. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Time'.]

predicate.spec: code under test reads the current time through an injectable/substitutable seam rather than calling the system clock directly, so tests can freeze it to a known value.

rules.text: Remote/network calls at test time are a leading non-determinism source. Replace the remote system with a test double that mimics its behavior under your control; guard against the double drifting out of sync with reality by running contract tests — the same interaction test run against both the fake and the real service. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Remote Services', and martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — 'Integration With Separate Services'.]

predicate.spec: tests do not make live network calls to remote/external services; a test double stands in for the remote system, and a contract test independently verifies the double matches the real service's behavior.

rules.text: Resource leaks cause other, unrelated tests to fail intermittently. A good tactic: configure the pool to size 1 and make it throw when exhausted — so the first test that requests a resource after the leak fails, loudly and locally, instead of some innocent later test. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Resource Leaks'.]

predicate.spec: shared/managed test resources (e.g. connection pools) are constrained (e.g. pool size 1, throw-on-exhaustion) so a leak fails fast and attributes to the leaking test rather than surfacing as a random later failure.

rules.text: For asynchronous behavior, don't guess with fixed sleeps: expose an explicit hook the test can use to detect when the async operation has actually completed, and always pair any wait with a timeout, since the expected event might never arrive. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — footnotes on async completion hooks and timeouts.]

predicate.spec: tests that wait on asynchronous work use an explicit completion signal/hook rather than a fixed sleep, and every such wait has a timeout guarding against the event never occurring.

rules.text: Test coverage is 'a useful tool for finding untested parts of a codebase' — and 'of little use as a numeric statement of how good your tests are.' These are two different claims; conflating them is the mistake. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html.]

predicate.spec: coverage output is used to locate untested code paths, and coverage percentage alone is not treated as a proxy for overall test quality.

rules.text: Brian Marick's distinction, quoted approvingly by Fowler: 'I expect a high level of coverage. Sometimes managers require one. There's a subtle difference.' A coverage number you notice is diagnostic information; a coverage number you're required to hit is a quota, and quotas get gamed. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html, quoting Brian Marick.]

predicate.spec: coverage is treated as an expectation/signal to investigate deviations from, not a mandated numeric gate that must be hit to pass a build or review.

rules.text: Making coverage a hard target invites low-quality tests that only exist to move the number — Fowler names this failure mode 'AssertionFreeTesting': tests that execute code (raising coverage) without ever actually checking anything. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html.]

predicate.spec: no test in the suite exercises code purely to raise a coverage number without making any assertion about the resulting behavior.

rules.text: Property-based testing: instead of hand-picking example inputs, write a test that should hold for all inputs in a described range/strategy, and let the tool randomly generate which of those inputs to actually check — including edge cases you might not have thought of yourself. [VERIFIED, hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html.]

predicate.spec: a property-based test asserts an invariant/property over a generated range of inputs (via a strategy/generator), rather than asserting on one or a few hand-picked example inputs.

rules.text: Property-based testing is explicitly 'a powerful addition to unit testing. It is not always a replacement.' Good candidate properties: round-trip behavior, equivalence between an optimized implementation and a slower-but-obviously-correct reference, invariants that must always hold, and no-crash-on-valid-input for parsers/linters/compilers. [VERIFIED, hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/introduction.html — 'When to use Hypothesis and property-based testing'.]

predicate.spec: property-based tests coexist with example-based unit tests rather than replacing them, and target one of: round-trip, reference-implementation equivalence, an always-true invariant, or no-crash-on-valid-input.

rules.text: When a property-based run finds a counterexample, it reports the actual failing input, which is often already small and pointed (e.g., a documented Hypothesis run against a sort function over mixed integers/floats reported the counterexample [1.0, nan, 0], immediately exposing that sorting in the presence of nan is ill-defined). [VERIFIED, hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/introduction.html — 'Preventing floats() from generating nan'.]

predicate.spec: a property-based test failure report includes a concrete, specific counterexample input the developer can reason about directly, not merely a pass/fail summary.

rules.text: Property-based testing frameworks (Hypothesis included) are generally understood to shrink a randomly-found failing case down toward the smallest/simplest input that still reproduces the failure, before reporting it. [INFERRED] — this is the framework's well-known general behavior; the specific pages fetched this session illustrate a small counterexample but do not themselves spell out the shrinking algorithm in the retrieved text.
rules.reviewer_criterion: When relying on or explaining a property-based testing tool's reported counterexample, is the fact that it was likely shrunk toward a minimal reproducer treated as a general, tool-dependent behavior to verify per-tool, rather than asserted as directly confirmed for every framework?

rules.text: Snapshot testing (also called golden-file or approval testing) captures a serialized rendering of some output the first time a test runs, storing it as a snapshot/golden file; on every later run, the current output is compared against that stored file and any difference fails the test. This is a general technique implemented across many ecosystems under compatible names, not a Jest-only idea: Jest for JavaScript/TypeScript (used as this guide's one labelled example), insta for Rust, pytest snapshot/syntax-tree plugins for Python, and ApprovalTests — a multi-language family (Java, .NET, C++, Python, Ruby, Go, and more). [VERIFIED, jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing — 'a very useful tool whenever you want to make sure your UI [or other output] does not change unexpectedly'; VERIFIED, insta.rs — 'Snapshots tests (also sometimes called approval tests) are tests that assert values against a reference value (the snapshot)'; VERIFIED, approvaltests.com — 'Approvaltests is in many languages,' listing 15 language implementations.]

predicate.spec: a snapshot test compares current output against a previously stored snapshot artifact and fails on any diff, rather than asserting against hand-written expected values each time; the mechanism is available in some form (snapshot/golden-file/approval library) in the project's language, not assumed to require Jest specifically.

rules.text: Treat the snapshot/golden artifact as code: commit it alongside the change that produced it, and review it as part of code review. Good snapshot tooling deliberately renders the stored value in a human-readable format so a reviewer can read the diff — Jest's version of this is pretty-format (this rule's labelled example); the same discipline is not Jest-specific — insta independently documents rendering readable terminal diffs. [VERIFIED, jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing, as the labelled example; VERIFIED, insta.rs — 'Pretty Diffs: insta renders beautiful snapshot diffs right in your terminal,' confirming the discipline generalizes beyond Jest.]

predicate.spec: snapshot files are committed to version control alongside the code change that produced them, and snapshot diffs are part of the code review, not auto-approved, regardless of which language's snapshot tool is in use.

rules.text: Any non-deterministic field in the snapshotted value (generated ids, timestamps) will fail the snapshot on every run unless normalized — snapshot tooling generally provides some form of placeholder/redaction mechanism so a matcher, not the literal generated value, is what gets checked and stored. Jest's version is an asymmetric property matcher (e.g. expect.any(Date), this rule's labelled example); insta calls the equivalent mechanism a redaction. [VERIFIED, jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing — 'Property Matchers', as the labelled example; VERIFIED, insta.rs — 'Redactions: if you have output which can change between test runs (such as random identifiers, timestamps or others) you can instruct insta to redact these parts,' confirming the same normalization need recurs outside Jest.]

predicate.spec: non-deterministic fields (ids, timestamps, random values) inside a snapshotted value are replaced with a matcher or redaction placeholder (whatever the project's snapshot tool provides) before snapshotting, rather than being snapshotted as literal values.

rules.text: A snapshot test verifies 'did the output change,' not 'is the output correct.' Because tooling commonly offers an interactive mode to step through and accept/reject each failed snapshot (Jest's Interactive Snapshot Mode is this rule's labelled example; insta's cargo-insta review flow is the equivalent in Rust), it is easy to rubber-stamp every diff without reading it — which defeats the purpose. A human must judge each diff at the moment it's created. [INFERRED, drawn from Jest's and insta's documented review workflows — the docs describe the mechanism; the discipline required is this guide's synthesis.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: When a snapshot test fails and the diff is reviewed, is each changed line actually read and judged as intentional-and-correct before accepting the new snapshot, rather than bulk-accepting every failed snapshot in interactive mode?

rules.text: The standard reaction to a production bug in a team practicing self-testing code: first write a test that exposes the bug, and only then try to fix it. Writing that test may itself be a series of tests that progressively narrow the scope down to a single unit test that reliably triggers the bug. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfTestingCode.html.]

predicate.spec: for a reported bug, a failing test that reproduces it is written and confirmed to fail before any fix is written.

rules.text: 'Any bug isn't just a failure in the code, it's equally a failure in the testing screen.' Writing the reproducing test first is not only a debugging technique — it is what guarantees the bug stays fixed, since a later regression will now be caught automatically instead of silently reintroduced. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfTestingCode.html, verbatim.]

predicate.spec: every fixed bug leaves behind a permanent regression test in the suite that would fail again if the bug were reintroduced.

rules.text: Use a fixed bug as a trigger to audit for sibling untested cases nearby — a team practicing this well treats one discovered bug as inspiration to look for similar missing tests, not just an isolated data point to patch and move past. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfTestingCode.html.]
rules.reviewer_criterion: After fixing a bug and adding its regression test, was a deliberate check made for structurally similar untested cases nearby, rather than closing the issue as soon as the one reported case passes?

rules.text: An uncontrolled non-deterministic test doesn't just cost the one flaky result — it degrades the whole suite's signal, until 'people don't pay much attention to whether [tests] pass or fail.' A suite nobody trusts has already failed at its job, whatever its pass/fail count says. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html.]

predicate.spec: the team's actual behavior toward test failures (investigating and blocking on them) matches what the suite's pass/fail status is supposed to mean — failures are not routinely ignored or re-run-until-green.

rules.text: Kent Beck's Test Desiderata names both the speed and the confidence properties directly: Fast — 'tests should run quickly'; Inspiring — 'passing the tests should inspire confidence.' A suite that is slow enough to be skipped, or unreliable enough to be ignored, satisfies neither. [VERIFIED, Kent Beck, 'Test Desiderata,' medium.com/@kentbeck_7670/test-desiderata-94150638a4b3.]

predicate.spec: the test suite runs fast enough, and reliably enough, that developers actually run it and act on a passing/failing result rather than skipping or discounting it.

rules.text: Generalize 'pristine' beyond flakiness to any accumulating source of noise a team learns to tune out — stale skipped tests, ignored warnings, tests nobody remembers the purpose of. Anything a developer has learned to routinely disregard in the test output has, functionally, stopped being part of the suite's signal even while it's still nominally 'passing.' [INFERRED] — a generalization of Fowler's quarantine/trust argument (tdd-44, tdd-64) beyond the specific non-determinism case it was made for.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is there any category of test-suite noise (skipped tests, warnings, dead assertions) that the team has learned to routinely ignore, and if so is it being actively cleaned up rather than left to accumulate as tolerated background noise?

rules.text: Quarantine (tdd-44) is a tool for preserving trust in the healthy suite while you fix the broken part — it is not a place to let a test live forever. Bound it explicitly (a count limit or a time limit) so hitting the bound forces the cleanup work rather than letting quarantine quietly grow. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html — 'Quarantine'.]

predicate.spec: the quarantine area for flaky tests has an explicit, enforced bound (count or time) that triggers mandatory cleanup once reached.

rules.text: Refactoring is a named, bounded step of the cycle — 'refactor both new and old code to make it well structured' — not an ongoing background activity done whenever you feel like it mid-implementation. It happens after green, as its own deliberate pass. [VERIFIED, martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html.]

predicate.spec: structural rework is performed as its own explicit step after the current test is green, not interleaved arbitrarily with getting a test to pass.

rules.text: The reason refactoring is sequenced strictly after green: correct behavior and correct structure are two goals a limited mind cannot optimize simultaneously, so the discipline is to nail behavior first (with the safety net of a passing test), and only then restructure with that safety net intact. [VERIFIED, blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/12/17/TheCyclesOfTDD.html.]

predicate.spec: whenever refactoring is in progress, there is already a passing test suite in place acting as the safety net for that restructuring.

rules.text: Never expand behavior during a refactor step. If new behavior is needed while refactoring, that observation belongs on the test list (tdd-5) as the seed of the next red-green cycle — not folded into the refactor already in progress. A refactor is only provably safe if the tests it runs under didn't change what they were checking. [INFERRED] — the direct corollary of tdd-68/tdd-69's behavior-then-structure sequencing.
rules.reviewer_criterion: During a refactor step, is the change strictly behavior-preserving (no new test assertions or new behavior introduced), with any newly noticed behavior need deferred to a fresh red-green cycle instead of being folded into the refactor?

rules.text: Randomized and property-based tests must record — and be able to replay — the seed that produced a failure. A failure surfaced by generated/random input is only as trustworthy as the suite's other determinism guarantees (tdd-3, tdd-43) if it is deterministically reproducible rather than a one-off; a randomized test that fails, is re-run, and passes without anyone capturing what input caused the failure is a non-determinism problem wearing a different hat. Property-based frameworks provide this directly: Hypothesis (this rule's labelled example) prints the failing seed and lets you pin it with @seed(...) or pytest's --hypothesis-seed, and separately auto-saves failing examples to a local database so they replay via @example / @reproduce_failure (see §11) — the same expectation generalizes to any other property-based or fuzz-style test runner, not just Hypothesis. [VERIFIED, hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/api.html — hypothesis.seed(seed): 'Seed the randomness for this test... for a fixed seed value Hypothesis will produce the same test cases... If using pytest, you can alternatively pass --hypothesis-seed on the command line'; VERIFIED, hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/replaying-failures.html — 'When a test fails, Hypothesis automatically saves the failure so it can be replayed later,' via its ExampleDatabase, @example, and @reproduce_failure.]

predicate.spec: a randomized/property-based test that fails records (via a printed seed, saved example, or equivalent artifact) enough information to deterministically replay the exact failing case on demand, rather than the failure being treated as reproduced only by chance on a future run.
